summary: For ages 6–7, children investigate how light passes through everyday materials and classify them as transparent (a clear image gets through), translucent (some light gets through as a blurry glow, no clear image) or opaque (no light gets through). The central goal is procedural: run a fair darkened-room torch test and sort materials by the observed light result, holding the translucent MIDDLE category distinct rather than collapsing into a see-through / not-see-through binary. Children judge by the light and image that come through the material onto a screen or to the eye (never by looking into the beam or toward the sun through a material) and anchor the vocabulary to what they witness, not to how a material looks.
misconceptions: 'All materials that let light through them are transparent' — collapsing translucent into transparent.
Transparent vs opaque is a strict binary with no partial 'some light through' middle.
Judging whether light passes by appearance alone instead of actively testing.
'Opaque' means dark-coloured, rather than 'blocks light' (so a thick white material isn't recognised as opaque).
A material is either see-through or not as a fixed label, ignoring that thickness/layering changes how much light passes.

activities.title: Torch-beam classification: build a fair test and sort materials
steps: In a darkened room, use a torch to light a small object or picture, then test each material by holding it between the lit object and your eye, or by shining the torch through it onto a white screen or wall.

Judge each material by the light and image that come THROUGH it — the image reaching your eye or the patch of light on the screen. Do not stare into the torch beam, and never look toward the sun through any material.

Decide for each material whether you can see the object CLEARLY (transparent), see only a blurry glow with no clear image (translucent), or see nothing because the light is blocked (opaque). If you are using the screen instead, look at the patch of light: a bright patch with sharp edges, almost the same as with no material (transparent); a dimmer, fuzzy glow (translucent); or a dark shadow with no light (opaque).
Test at least six materials, for example clear plastic or glass, tracing or greaseproof paper, frosted plastic, cardboard, a thin cloth, and a wooden block.
Keep the test fair: same torch, same distance, same screen, same dark conditions for every material.
Predict each material's group first, then run the test and check your prediction against what the light actually does.
Sort each material into a three-column chart: TRANSPARENT / TRANSLUCENT / OPAQUE, and record your results in a table.
activities.insight: Materials fall into three light-transmitting groups, not two. The crucial middle case is translucent: it lets light through (so a child may expect 'transparent') but you cannot see a clear image through it — only a fuzzy glow — so it belongs in its own category. The group is decided by what the light does as it comes through the material, not by how the material looks.

activities.title: Classify-and-define follow-on check
steps: Match each term — transparent, translucent, opaque — to its definition: light passes through clearly; some light passes but blurry, no clear image; no light passes.
Given a set of materials, sort each into transparent / translucent / opaque.
For a named material, predict whether light will pass through and whether you would expect to see a clear image, a glow, or nothing — then test it where possible.
activities.insight: Consolidates the three vocabulary terms and their observable meanings, confirming the learner holds a distinct translucent category and can apply the terms to new materials.

activities.title: Introduce the three words with a labelled light scene
steps: Look at a labelled display showing materials already sorted into transparent, translucent and opaque, and tap or reveal each label.
Say each new word aloud and recall which group means a clear image, which a blurry glow, and which no light.
activities.insight: Pre-teaches or reinforces the three terms before or alongside hands-on testing, so the vocabulary is available when children run and describe their own tests.

checkQuestion: Here is a torch and a tray of materials (clear plastic, tracing/greaseproof paper, cardboard, thin fabric, frosted plastic, a wooden block). In a dimmed room, set up your own test to shine the torch through each material onto a white screen, and sort the materials into three groups: light passes through clearly, some light passes but blurry, and no light passes. Decide each material's group and label the three groups.
checkAnswer: A fair, consistent test (same torch, same distance, same screen) that sorts clear plastic as transparent (a sharp bright patch / a clear image gets through), tracing and frosted plastic as translucent (a glow gets through but no clear image), and cardboard, wood and thick fabric as opaque (light blocked, a sharp shadow). The child uses the three terms correctly.
